claim: Dynamin catalyzes membrane fission in eukaryotic cells.
source: The large GTPase dynamin catalyzes membrane fission in eukaryotic cells, but despite three decades of experimental work, competing and partially conflicting models persist regarding some of its most basic actions.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract, representing consensus knowledge in the field.

claim: Competing and partially conflicting models persist regarding dynamin's most basic actions despite three decades of experimental work.
source: The large GTPase dynamin catalyzes membrane fission in eukaryotic cells, but despite three decades of experimental work, competing and partially conflicting models persist regarding some of its most basic actions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, representing an inference from the literature.

claim: An effective rotation of the dynamin filament around its longitudinal axis reflects alternate tilting of dynamin's PH binding domains and creates a membrane torque.
source: Beyond changes of radius and pitch, we emphasize the crucial role of a third functional motion: an effective rotation of the filament around its longitudinal axis, which reflects alternate tilting of dynamin's PH binding domains and creates a membrane torque.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulation study presented in the manuscript.

claim: Helix elongation impedes fission.
source: We also show that helix elongation impedes fission, hemifission is reached via a small transient pore, and coat disassembly assists fission.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulation study, supported by data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Hemifission is reached via a small transient pore.
source: We also show that helix elongation impedes fission, hemifission is reached via a small transient pore, and coat disassembly assists fission.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulation study, supported by data shown in Figure 2h and Figure 4.

claim: Coat disassembly assists fission.
source: We also show that helix elongation impedes fission, hemifission is reached via a small transient pore, and coat disassembly assists fission.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulation study, supported by data shown in Videos 5 and 6.

claim: Of the three 80% homologous mammalian isoforms of dynamin, Dyn1, highly expressed in neurons, has been studied best.
source: Of the three 80% homologous mammalian isoforms of dynamin, Dyn1, highly expressed in neurons, has been studied best (Hinshaw, 2000; Praefcke and McMahon, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dynamin monomers oligomerize via their stalks in a criss-cross fashion, resulting in stable dimers or tetramers in solution.
source: Dynamin monomers oligomerize via their stalks in a criss-cross fashion, resulting in stable dimers (Cocucci et al., 2014) or tetramers (Ramachandran et al., 2007) in solution.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Continuing the assembly path of dynamin oligomers yields helical filaments.
source: Continuing this assembly path yields helical filaments (Carr and Hinshaw, 1997), which have an outer diameter of about 50 nm and a helical pitch (i.e., height increment during one complete helical turn) between 10 nm and 20 nm in the absence of GTP (Chen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Dynamin helical filaments have an outer diameter of about 50 nm and a helical pitch between 10 nm and 20 nm in the absence of GTP.
source: Continuing this assembly path yields helical filaments (Carr and Hinshaw, 1997), which have an outer diameter of about 50 nm and a helical pitch (i.e., height increment during one complete helical turn) between 10 nm and 20 nm in the absence of GTP (Chen et al., 2004).
evidence: This structural information is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Specific interactions among dynamin subunits are not conserved throughout the large dynamin superfamily, yet all members share similar architectural assembly properties.
source: Specific interactions among dynamin subunits are not conserved throughout the large dynamin superfamily, yet all members share similar architectural assembly properties (Praefcke and McMahon, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the two-stage model, nucleotide-loaded dynamin assembles into highly constricted helices, whose entrapped lipid tubules spontaneously undergo hemifission.
source: In the two-stage model (Bashkirov et al., 2008; Mattila et al., 2015), nucleotide-loaded dynamin assembles into highly constricted helices, whose entrapped lipid tubules spontaneously undergo hemifission; GTP hydrolysis induces subsequent detachment of the dynamin scaffold from the membrane, allowing the hemifission state to proceed to complete fission.
evidence: This describes a model from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: In the two-stage model, GTP hydrolysis induces subsequent detachment of the dynamin scaffold from the membrane, allowing the hemifission state to proceed to complete fission.
source: In the two-stage model (Bashkirov et al., 2008; Mattila et al., 2015), nucleotide-loaded dynamin assembles into highly constricted helices, whose entrapped lipid tubules spontaneously undergo hemifission; GTP hydrolysis induces subsequent detachment of the dynamin scaffold from the membrane, allowing the hemifission state to proceed to complete fission.
evidence: This describes a model from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The lack of dynamin's cooperativity with GTP during hydrolysis is not compatible with key requirements of the two-stage model.
source: However, neither the lack of dynamin's cooperativity with GTP during hydrolysis (Tuma and Collins, 1994), nor the short lifetime of the post-hydrolysis GDP + Pi state (Antonny et al., 2016) are compatible with key requirements of the two-stage model.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited experimental findings that contradict the two-stage model.

claim: The short lifetime of the post-hydrolysis GDP + Pi state is not compatible with key requirements of the two-stage model.
source: However, neither the lack of dynamin's cooperativity with GTP during hydrolysis (Tuma and Collins, 1994), nor the short lifetime of the post-hydrolysis GDP + Pi state (Antonny et al., 2016) are compatible with key requirements of the two-stage model.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited experimental findings that contradict the two-stage model.

claim: It remains unclear why the experimentally observed superconstricted state does not reach hemifission.
source: It also remains unclear why the experimentally observed superconstricted state does not reach hemifission.
evidence: This is a statement about an unresolved question in the field.

claim: In the constrictase model, several cycles of GTP hydrolysis induce adjacent turns to stepwise slide past one another, actively constricting the helix and its enclosed membrane tube until the latter fissions.
source: In the constrictase model (Chappie et al., 2011), several cycles of GTP hydrolysis induce adjacent turns (or 'rungs') to stepwise slide past one another, actively constricting the helix and its enclosed membrane tube until the latter fissions; disassembly is then a consequence of the vanishing lipid substrate.
evidence: This describes a model from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: In the constrictase model, disassembly is a consequence of the vanishing lipid substrate.
source: In the constrictase model (Chappie et al., 2011), several cycles of GTP hydrolysis induce adjacent turns (or 'rungs') to stepwise slide past one another, actively constricting the helix and its enclosed membrane tube until the latter fissions; disassembly is then a consequence of the vanishing lipid substrate.
evidence: This describes a model from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The cryo-EM density of stalks in a constricted 2-start helix does not match the X-ray structure of dimers.
source: The problems here are that the cryo-EM density of stalks in a constricted (albeit: 2-start) helix does not match the X-ray structure of dimers, that it is not known how G-G links across rungs would unbind and step cooperatively, and that the mechanics of the final disassembly is less clear (Antonny et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a problem with the constrictase model, supported by a citation.

claim: It is not known how G-G links across rungs would unbind and step cooperatively in the constrictase model.
source: The problems here are that the cryo-EM density of stalks in a constricted (albeit: 2-start) helix does not match the X-ray structure of dimers, that it is not known how G-G links across rungs would unbind and step cooperatively, and that the mechanics of the final disassembly is less clear (Antonny et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a problem with the constrictase model, supported by a citation.

claim: The mechanics of the final disassembly in the constrictase model is less clear.
source: The problems here are that the cryo-EM density of stalks in a constricted (albeit: 2-start) helix does not match the X-ray structure of dimers, that it is not known how G-G links across rungs would unbind and step cooperatively, and that the mechanics of the final disassembly is less clear (Antonny et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a problem with the constrictase model, supported by a citation.

claim: Theoretical calculations have provided constraints on energetics and morphology but assume high symmetries and ignore fluctuations.
source: Theoretical calculations have provided constraints on energetics and morphology (Kozlov, 1999; Kozlovsky and Kozlov, 2003; Bashkirov et al., 2008; McDargh et al., 2016; McDargh and Deserno, 2018), but these assume high symmetries and ignore fluctuations.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of prior theoretical work, supported by citations.

claim: Recent coarse-grained simulations in which the dynamin helix is represented as a pair of rings have elucidated the relevance of local torques.
source: Recent coarse-grained (CG) simulations, in which the dynamin helix is represented as a pair of rings, have elucidated the relevance of local torques (Fuhrmans and Müller, 2015) and the possibility of long-lived hemifission intermediates (Mattila et al., 2015; Zhang and Müller, 2017), but the implied mirror symmetry differs from the actual helicoidal one.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior simulation studies.

claim: Recent coarse-grained simulations in which the dynamin helix is represented as a pair of rings have elucidated the possibility of long-lived hemifission intermediates.
source: Recent coarse-grained (CG) simulations, in which the dynamin helix is represented as a pair of rings, have elucidated the relevance of local torques (Fuhrmans and Müller, 2015) and the possibility of long-lived hemifission intermediates (Mattila et al., 2015; Zhang and Müller, 2017), but the implied mirror symmetry differs from the actual helicoidal one.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior simulation studies.

claim: The mirror symmetry implied by representing dynamin as a pair of rings differs from the actual helicoidal symmetry.
source: Recent coarse-grained (CG) simulations, in which the dynamin helix is represented as a pair of rings, have elucidated the relevance of local torques (Fuhrmans and Müller, 2015) and the possibility of long-lived hemifission intermediates (Mattila et al., 2015; Zhang and Müller, 2017), but the implied mirror symmetry differs from the actual helicoidal one.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of prior models.

claim: The CG membrane model captures a well-placed pivotal plane.
source: The emergent CG membranes capture not only a wide range of mesoscopic phenomena (Deserno, 2009), but also very local bilayer properties that likely play a role during leaflet-breaking fission events, such as a well-placed pivotal plane (Wang and Deserno, 2015), a correct magnitude and correlation length for lipid tilt (Wang and Deserno, 2016), and a pore-opening scenario (Cooke et al., 2005; Deserno, 2009) in agreement with previous simulations and continuum theory (Farago, 2003; Tolpekina et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a property of the simulation model, supported by citations.

claim: The CG membrane model captures a correct magnitude and correlation length for lipid tilt.
source: The emergent CG membranes capture not only a wide range of mesoscopic phenomena (Deserno, 2009), but also very local bilayer properties that likely play a role during leaflet-breaking fission events, such as a well-placed pivotal plane (Wang and Deserno, 2015), a correct magnitude and correlation length for lipid tilt (Wang and Deserno, 2016), and a pore-opening scenario (Cooke et al., 2005; Deserno, 2009) in agreement with previous simulations and continuum theory (Farago, 2003; Tolpekina et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a property of the simulation model, supported by citations.

claim: The CG membrane model's pore-opening scenario is in agreement with previous simulations and continuum theory.
source: The emergent CG membranes capture not only a wide range of mesoscopic phenomena (Deserno, 2009), but also very local bilayer properties that likely play a role during leaflet-breaking fission events, such as a well-placed pivotal plane (Wang and Deserno, 2015), a correct magnitude and correlation length for lipid tilt (Wang and Deserno, 2016), and a pore-opening scenario (Cooke et al., 2005; Deserno, 2009) in agreement with previous simulations and continuum theory (Farago, 2003; Tolpekina et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a validation of the simulation model, supported by citations.

claim: The simulations start with a pre-formed helix winding around the neck of an elongated vesicle comprising about 10,000 lipids.
source: In the present study we forgo the dynamin assembly process and start with a pre-formed helix winding around the neck of an elongated vesicle comprising about 10,000 lipids (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation setup, supported by Figure 1c.

claim: The scaffold geometry is changed by tuning the equilibrium distances between its CG beads, imposing internal stresses that trigger a global elastic shape relaxation.
source: We change the scaffold geometry by tuning the equilibrium distances between its CG beads, that is by imposing internal stresses that trigger a global elastic shape relaxation, and we do this slowly enough to avoid viscous stresses in the bilayer (Figure 6, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation protocol, supported by Figure 6.

claim: All simulations were performed using the ESPResSo package.
source: All simulations were performed using the ESPResSo package (Limbach et al., 2006) and run in triplicate, leading to consistent results.
evidence: This is a methodological detail, supported by a citation.

claim: All simulations were run in triplicate, leading to consistent results.
source: All simulations were performed using the ESPResSo package (Limbach et al., 2006) and run in triplicate, leading to consistent results.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about reproducibility.

claim: Visualization was done with VMD.
source: Visualization was done with VMD (Humphrey et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a methodological detail, supported by a citation.

claim: At a confinement approximately corresponding to the superconstricted state, the enclosed membrane tube remains stable during pure constriction.
source: At a confinement approximately corresponding to the superconstricted state, the enclosed membrane tube remains stable.
evidence: This is a finding from the pure constriction simulations.

claim: In the pure constriction case, the hemifission intermediate only forms at constriction levels that eliminate the inner lumen.
source: The hemifission intermediate only forms at constriction levels that eliminate the inner lumen (Figure 2f, blue curve, and Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the pure constriction simulations, supported by Figure 2f and Video 1.

claim: Kozlovsky and Kozlov (2003) found that an inner lumen diameter smaller than approximately 2 nm should spontaneously proceed towards hemifission.
source: This seems to contradict the findings by Kozlovsky and Kozlov (2003) that an inner lumen diameter smaller than approximately 2 nm should spontaneously proceed towards hemifission, but this is not so: in their study an approximately catenoidal neck fissions by the application of bending moments at the upper and lower edge of the neck, while in our case the neck is created by external constriction—a mechanically different scenario.
evidence: This is a finding from prior literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The mechanical scenario in Kozlovsky and Kozlov (2003) differs from the present study: in their study an approximately catenoidal neck fissions by the application of bending moments at the upper and lower edge of the neck, while in the present case the neck is created by external constriction.
source: This seems to contradict the findings by Kozlovsky and Kozlov (2003) that an inner lumen diameter smaller than approximately 2 nm should spontaneously proceed towards hemifission, but this is not so: in their study an approximately catenoidal neck fissions by the application of bending moments at the upper and lower edge of the neck, while in our case the neck is created by external constriction—a mechanically different scenario.
evidence: This is an inference explaining the difference between the present results and prior work.

claim: The dynamin-coated superconstricted lipid tubule is stable in experiment.
source: Indeed, the dynamin-coated superconstricted lipid tubule is stable in experiment (Sundborger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by a citation.

claim: Some experiments have shown that GTP hydrolysis may increase the filament's pitch at fixed radius.
source: Some experiments have shown that GTP hydrolysis may increase the filament's pitch at fixed radius (Figure 2d), which has led to the suggestion that dynamin might act as an extension spring ('poppase model') (Stowell et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by a citation and Figure 2d.

claim: The observation that GTP hydrolysis may increase the filament's pitch at fixed radius has led to the suggestion that dynamin might act as an extension spring ('poppase model').
source: Some experiments have shown that GTP hydrolysis may increase the filament's pitch at fixed radius (Figure 2d), which has led to the suggestion that dynamin might act as an extension spring ('poppase model') (Stowell et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a model from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Dynamin changes its shape slowly compared to a membrane's viscoelastic time scale, believed to be shorter than about 10 ms.
source: However, since dynamin changes its shape slowly compared to a membrane's viscoelastic time scale, believed to be shorter than about 10 ms (Camley and Brown, 2011), this putative mechanism cannot rely on viscous stresses but instead only on the reversible work being performed during elongation of the neck.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited knowledge about membrane viscoelastic time scales.

claim: The poppase mechanism cannot rely on viscous stresses but instead only on the reversible work being performed during elongation of the neck.
source: However, since dynamin changes its shape slowly compared to a membrane's viscoelastic time scale, believed to be shorter than about 10 ms (Camley and Brown, 2011), this putative mechanism cannot rely on viscous stresses but instead only on the reversible work being performed during elongation of the neck.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time scales involved.

claim: Helical elongation impedes fission because a large pitch prevents the helical filament from symmetrically confining the membrane, allowing it to 'bulge out' at the open groove.
source: This happens because a large pitch prevents the helical filament from symmetrically confining the membrane, allowing it to 'bulge out' at the open groove (Figure 2f, dark blue curve).
evidence: This is an explanation for the finding, supported by Figure 2f.

claim: In nature, membrane bulging at the open groove could be prevented by accessory proteins, or by the second interlocking filament if the two-start helix is physiologically relevant.
source: In nature this could be prevented by accessory proteins, or—if the two-start helix is physiologically relevant—by the second interlocking filament.
evidence: This is a speculation about how the system might work in vivo.

claim: Mehrotra et al. (2014) have shown that a change in PH domain orientation may regulate fission.
source: Mehrotra et al. (2014) have shown that a change in PH domain orientation may regulate fission.
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by a citation.

claim: Sundborger et al. (2014) fitted dynamin's crystallographic structure to EM density maps and noticed that one of the two PH domains per dimer tilts out of the membrane, thereby breaking the symmetry of the dimer.
source: Sundborger et al. (2014) fitted dynamin's crystallographic structure to EM density maps and noticed that one of the two PH domains per dimer tilts out of the membrane, thereby breaking the symmetry of the dimer.
evidence: This is a structural finding, supported by a citation.

claim: A 3.75 Å resolution Cryo-EM reconstruction of human Dyn1 in the GMPPCP-bound state shows that the bundle signaling element (BSE) is asymmetrically bent, presumably due to forces generated from the GTPase dimer interaction.
source: And a very recent 3.75 Å resolution Cryo-EM reconstruction of human Dyn1 in the GMPPCP-bound state (Kong et al., 2018) shows that the bundle signaling element (BSE) is asymmetrically bent, presumably due to forces generated from the GTPase dimer interaction.
evidence: This is a structural finding, supported by a citation.

claim: Forces from the GTPase dimer interaction are transferred across the stalk to the PH domain and onto the lipid membrane.
source: These forces are further transferred across the stalk to the PH domain and onto the lipid membrane.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural findings of Kong et al. (2018).

claim: Local rearrangement of the tertiary structure can effectively be described as a net rotation of the helical scaffold around its local longitudinal axis on mesoscopic scales.
source: On mesoscopic scales, this local rearrangement of the tertiary structure can effectively be described as a net rotation of the helical scaffold around its local longitudinal axis, even if the core of the protein filament does not actually co-rotate.
evidence: This is an inference about how to represent the structural changes in a coarse-grained model.

claim: If the PH domains of each monomer were to tilt in the same fashion, then due to dynamin's criss-cross assembly half of the PH domains would tilt 'up' while the other half would tilt 'down', which on average does not displace the filament's binding surface.
source: If the PH domains of each monomer were to tilt in the same fashion, then due to dynamin's criss-cross assembly half of the PH domains would tilt 'up' while the other half would tilt 'down', which on average does not displace the filament's binding surface.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of symmetric PH domain tilting.

claim: If only one of the two sets of PH domains tilts, this breaks the up-down symmetry and effectively rotates the average position of the adhesive strip away from the substrate.
source: However, if only one of these two sets of PH domains tilts, this breaks the up-down symmetry and—at the level of our CG model—effectively rotates the average position of the adhesive strip away from the substrate.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of asymmetric PH domain tilting.

claim: Asymmetric PH domain tilting creates a tangential torque on the membrane because adhesion pins the filament's local material frame to its Darboux frame on the surface.
source: This creates a tangential torque on the membrane, because adhesion pins the filament's local material frame to its Darboux frame on the surface (Guven et al., 2014), and therefore it has appropriately been called 'Darboux torque' (Fierling et al., 2016)—see Figure 2g and Box 1.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited theoretical work, supported by Figure 2g.

claim: The tangential torque created by asymmetric PH domain tilting has been called 'Darboux torque'.
source: This creates a tangential torque on the membrane, because adhesion pins the filament's local material frame to its Darboux frame on the surface (Guven et al., 2014), and therefore it has appropriately been called 'Darboux torque' (Fierling et al., 2016)—see Figure 2g and Box 1.
evidence: This is a definition from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Kong et al. (2018) provide structural evidence that forces are transmitted all the way from dynamin's G-domain to the PH domain and onto the membrane.
source: However, there is also a second problem: it is by no means obvious how a highly curved bilayer responds to the forces and torques imposed by such complex geometric constraints. Theoretical calculations have provided constraints on energetics and morphology (Kozlov, 1999; Kozlovsky and Kozlov, 2003; Bashkirov et al., 2008; McDargh et al., 2016; McDargh and Deserno, 2018), but these assume high symmetries and ignore fluctuations. Recent coarse-grained (CG) simulations, in which the dynamin helix is represented as a pair of rings, have elucidated the relevance of local torques (Fuhrmans and Müller, 2015) and the possibility of long-lived hemifission intermediates (Mattila et al., 2015; Zhang and Müller, 2017), but the implied mirror symmetry differs from the actual helicoidal one. Here we go beyond these studies and investigate the constriction of fluctuating lipid bilayer tubes by geometrically realistic dynamin helices.
evidence: This is a structural finding, supported by a citation.

claim: Neither the new structure by Kong et al. (2018), nor the previously observed tilting of the PH domain unambiguously proves the existence of torques.
source: Still, neither this new structure, nor the previously observed tilting of the PH domain (Sundborger et al., 2014) unambiguously proves the existence of torques.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of current structural evidence.

claim: The existence of a Darboux torque has been posited and exploited in another model for dynamin-driven fission, which simplifies the complex scaffold geometry to two counter-rotating apposing rings.
source: But while elucidating the mechanical nature of this process will have to await more detailed molecular modeling, the existence of a Darboux torque as been posited and exploited in another model for dynamin-driven fission, which simplifies the complex scaffold geometry to two counter-rotating apposing rings (Fuhrmans and Müller, 2015; Shnyrova et al., 2013), a geometry that remote-pinches the membrane between the rings.
evidence: This is a description of a prior model, supported by citations.

claim: Counter-rotating rings have a mirror symmetry and hence exert oppositely acting Darboux torques that constructively interfere in the middle of the scaffold.
source: Notice, though, that both geometry and symmetry are different in the latter case: counter-rotating rings have a mirror symmetry and hence exert oppositely acting Darboux torques that constructively interfere in the middle of the scaffold.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanics of the counter-rotating ring model.

claim: Since a helix is one contiguous filament, it will rotate everywhere in the same sense, rendering torque amplification much less straightforward than in the counter-rotating ring model.
source: Since a helix is one contiguous filament, it will rotate everywhere in the same sense, rendering torque amplification much less straightforward.
evidence: This is an inference about the difference between helical and ring geometries.

claim: Rotation is necessary for a constricted membrane tube with a remaining aqueous lumen to transition into the hemifission intermediate.
source: In our own simulations, which account for the full helical geometry, we find that rotation is necessary for a constricted membrane tube with a remaining aqueous lumen to transition into the hemifission intermediate.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: A non-rotating scaffold maintains adhesion while constricting, which could hold the membrane tube open and thereby prevent it from transitioning into the hemifission case.
source: Since rotation gradually diminishes binding between membrane and filament, a non-rotating scaffold maintains adhesion while constricting, which could hold the membrane tube open and thereby prevent it from transitioning into the hemifission case.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the simulation results.

claim: The functionally important consequence of rotation is not merely a reduction of binding energy, but active stresses, likely due to the Darboux torque.
source: This suggests that the functionally important consequence of rotation is not merely a reduction of binding energy, but active stresses, likely due to the above-mentioned Darboux torque.
evidence: This is an inference from the control simulation results.

claim: If in addition to constriction and rotation the helix is also elongated, hemifission is still reached before the inner lumen disappears, but this requires a further filament radius reduction.
source: If in addition to constriction and rotation we also elongate the helix, hemifission is still reached before the inner lumen disappears, but this requires a further filament radius reduction (Figure 2f, dark cyan curve).
evidence: This is a finding from the constriction + rotation + elongation simulations, supported by Figure 2f.

claim: The case with constriction, rotation, and elongation shows greater variability across the three runs, transitioning over three consecutive constriction steps.
source: Consistent with our observations on constriction plus elongation, this case with additional rotation also shows a greater variability across our three runs, transitioning over three consecutive constriction steps, which however fall between the bounds of constriction plus rotation and constriction only (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a finding about the variability of the simulation results, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Rotation supports hemifission, while elongation opposes it.
source: These findings again endorse the view that rotation supports hemifission, while elongation opposes it.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Pre-hemifission scaffold breakage aborts fission by allowing the enclosed membrane tube to re-expand.
source: We show that pre-hemifission scaffold breakage aborts fission by allowing the enclosed membrane tube to re-expand.
evidence: This is a finding from the scaffold disassembly simulations.

claim: Binding-capable fragments are individually not strong enough to impose their curvature on a substrate whose geometry becomes progressively unfavorable, and they ultimately detach from it.
source: Of note, even binding-capable fragments are individually not strong enough to impose their curvature on a substrate whose geometry becomes progressively unfavorable, and they ultimately detach from it.
evidence: This is a finding from the scaffold disassembly simulations.

claim: The scaffold only binds weakly, and rotation-driven hemifission is not the trivial result of massive forces resulting from large adhesion, or even of pulling lipids out of the membrane.
source: This also documents that our scaffold only binds weakly, and that rotation-driven hemifission is not the trivial result of massive forces resulting from large adhesion, or even of pulling lipids out of the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference from the scaffold disassembly simulations.

claim: The simulation setup does not exert external membrane tension, since the implicit solvent enforces no volume constraint and permits the membrane to relax the area per lipid.
source: Observe that our simulation setup does not exert external membrane tension, since our implicit solvent enforces no volume constraint and permits the membrane—even though closed and constricted—to relax the area per lipid.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation setup.

claim: A tension of a few mN/m approaches a membrane's rupture stress and would place the system dangerously close to unspecific bilayer failure.
source: Even disregarding the question how such a large tension would arise in a physiological context, the mere fact that this approaches a membrane's rupture stress and would hence place the system dangerously close to unspecific bilayer failure renders a recourse to such a high tension implausible.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of membrane mechanics.

claim: Dar et al. (2015) observed that fission of dynamin-coated membrane tubules occurs within the coated region.
source: Recent experiments have observed that fission of dynamin-coated membrane tubules occurs within the coated region (Dar et al., 2015), although earlier studies had suggested that fission occurs at the edge between the dynamin helix and the uncoated membrane (Morlot et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by a citation.

claim: Earlier studies had suggested that fission occurs at the edge between the dynamin helix and the uncoated membrane.
source: Recent experiments have observed that fission of dynamin-coated membrane tubules occurs within the coated region (Dar et al., 2015), although earlier studies had suggested that fission occurs at the edge between the dynamin helix and the uncoated membrane (Morlot et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by a citation.

claim: An initial hemifission seed appears in the middle of the neck for short filaments (up to 1.5 turns), or two seeds appear near the edges for longer ones (more than two turns).
source: We always observe that an initial hemifission seed appears in the middle of the neck for short filaments (up to 1.5 turns), or two seeds appear near the edges for longer ones (more than two turns), see Figure 2h.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, supported by Figure 2h.

claim: Two regions of highly localized stress appear slightly inwards of either edge of the filament, which overlap and may mutually amplify for sufficiently short filaments.
source: This suggests that two regions of highly localized stress appear slightly inwards of either edge, which overlap and may mutually amplify for sufficiently short filaments.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Fission is believed to be non-leaky.
source: That hemifission is seeded by a small pore is unexpected, not only because fission is believed to be non-leaky (Bashkirov et al., 2008), but also because the existence of a hemifission intermediate is generally taken to exclude the need for (or even possibility of) pores.
evidence: This is a statement about a belief in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: The existence of a hemifission intermediate is generally taken to exclude the need for (or even possibility of) pores.
source: That hemifission is seeded by a small pore is unexpected, not only because fission is believed to be non-leaky (Bashkirov et al., 2008), but also because the existence of a hemifission intermediate is generally taken to exclude the need for (or even possibility of) pores.
evidence: This is a statement about a belief in the field.

claim: The simulations suggest a non-axisymmetric pathway to hemifission: the filament seeds a small pore that widens around the circumference of the neck, while its top and bottom edges pull radially inward and fuse with the apposing intact membrane.
source: Our simulations suggest an intriguing non-axisymmetric pathway: the filament seeds a small pore that widens around the circumference of the neck, while its top and bottom edges pull radially inward and fuse with the apposing intact membrane.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: The non-axisymmetric pathway creates two defect lines at which three bilayers meet, and contracting them results in the top and bottom point singularity of the hemifission state's cylindrical micelle.
source: This creates two defect lines at which three bilayers meet, and contracting them results in the top and bottom point singularity of the hemifission state's cylindrical micelle.
evidence: This is a description of the pathway observed in the simulations.

claim: The non-axisymmetric pathway never involves a large pore, provided the filament stays short enough.
source: This sequence of events never involves a large pore, provided the filament stays short enough, a condition that imposes constraints on the constriction process itself.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: If dynamin constricts due to GTP hydrolysis, the initially unconstricted helix has to be long enough for the two rungs to meet, so that apposing G-domains can cross-catalyze hydrolysis.
source: If dynamin constricts due to GTP hydrolysis, as posited in the constrictase model, the initially unconstricted helix has to be long enough for the two rungs to meet, so that apposing G-domains can cross-catalyze hydrolysis.
evidence: This is an inference about the requirements of the constrictase model.

claim: Constricting the radius by a factor of two necessarily doubles the number of turns if the helical length stays fixed.
source: Constricting the radius by a factor of two then necessarily doubles the number of turns if the helical length stays fixed.
evidence: This is a geometric inference.

claim: Long scaffolds induce rather sizable pores that would likely result in leakage.
source: We find that such long scaffolds induce rather sizable pores (Figure 2h) that would likely result in leakage.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, supported by Figure 2h.

claim: The ends of a filament that in the constricted state only takes one turn would not be able to meet up in the preceding unconstricted state, and GTP driven constriction could not commence.
source: But the ends of a filament that in the constricted state only takes one turn would not be able to meet up in the preceding unconstricted state, and GTP driven constriction could not commence.
evidence: This is an inference about a constraint on the constrictase model.

claim: The dilemma of filament length could be resolved if constriction and disassembly happen in short succession.
source: This dilemma could be resolved if constriction and disassembly happen in short succession: when the two ends of the initially relaxed helical filament first meet, they hydrolyze GTP and trigger a first constriction step.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to resolve the constraint on the constrictase model.

claim: A filament end comprising ever longer stretches of spent dynamin can shed its monomers concurrently with the ongoing constriction, especially if its PH domain retracted from the membrane.
source: But since GTP hydrolysis enhances disassembly, a filament end comprising ever longer stretches of spent dynamin can shed its monomers concurrently with the ongoing constriction, especially if its PH domain retracted from the membrane.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how constriction and disassembly could be coordinated.

claim: The helix would tighten but never extend much beyond one turn if constriction and disassembly happen concurrently, and hence never induce large pores.
source: The helix would tighten but never extend much beyond one turn, and hence never induce large pores (Video 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with concurrent constriction and disassembly, supported by Video 5.

claim: The hypothesis of concurrent constriction and disassembly is compatible with the experimental evidence that, upon GTP hydrolysis, the scaffold seems to adjust to a length optimal for fission (about one full turn).
source: This hypothesis is compatible with the experimental evidence that, upon GTP hydrolysis, the scaffold seems to adjust to a length optimal for fission (about one full turn) (Shnyrova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of the hypothesis with experimental evidence, supported by a citation.

claim: Mattila et al. (2015) and Zhang and Müller (2017) find that the cylindrical micelle hemifission state is remarkably stable, suggesting that completing fission faces a very sizable second free energy barrier.
source: Without concurrent filament shortening, our hemifission state resembles a short cylindrical micelle (Figure 2f, background image), a transition state explored in two other recent investigations (Mattila et al., 2015; Zhang and Müller, 2017). These studies find that this micelle is remarkably stable, suggesting that completing fission faces a very sizable second free energy barrier.
evidence: This is a finding from prior simulation studies, supported by citations.

claim: In vitro experiments by Roux et al. (2006) and Morlot et al. (2012) have found that longitudinal tension assists in producing fission.
source: Additional tension might reduce its height, and indeed in vitro experiments by Roux et al. (2006) and Morlot et al. (2012) have found that longitudinal tension assists in producing fission (though it is interesting to note that our simulations present a tension-free pathway to fission).
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by citations.

claim: The present simulations present a tension-free pathway to fission.
source: Additional tension might reduce its height, and indeed in vitro experiments by Roux et al. (2006) and Morlot et al. (2012) have found that longitudinal tension assists in producing fission (though it is interesting to note that our simulations present a tension-free pathway to fission).
evidence: This is a finding from the present simulations.

claim: The second barrier to complete fission might not be biologically relevant, since it is a consequence of the simulation setup in prior studies, which prevents the micelle from shrinking and instead requires it to rupture mid-length.
source: Here we propose that this second barrier might indeed not be biologically relevant, since it is a consequence of the simulation setup in these studies, which prevents the micelle from shrinking and instead requires it to rupture mid-length.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the interpretation of prior simulation results.

claim: The simulations never observe the micelle to break while being enclosed by the dynamin scaffold.
source: In our simulations we also never observe the micelle to break while being enclosed by the dynamin scaffold (from which it has already unbound), but we argue that this is due to the scaffold preventing the two point defects at the end of the micelle from merging.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: The scaffold prevents the two point defects at the end of the micelle from merging.
source: In our simulations we also never observe the micelle to break while being enclosed by the dynamin scaffold (from which it has already unbound), but we argue that this is due to the scaffold preventing the two point defects at the end of the micelle from merging.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The force pulls the two daughter membranes together, whereupon bilayer contact catalyzes micellar fission.
source: This force pulls the two daughter membranes together, whereupon bilayer contact catalyzes micellar fission (see Video 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, supported by Video 6.

claim: Splitting the cylindrical micelle somewhere along its length would further raise the free energy by creating two spherical caps of even more unfavorable packing geometry.
source: This hypothesis, even though derived from a fairly coarse-grained model, is nevertheless plausible, because splitting the cylindrical micelle somewhere along its length would further raise the free energy by creating two spherical caps of even more unfavorable packing geometry (Zhang and Müller, 2017), while the contact between the daughter membranes annihilates the two already existing point defects at the micellar ends.
evidence: This is an inference based on membrane energetics, supported by a citation.

claim: The contact between the daughter membranes annihilates the two already existing point defects at the micellar ends.
source: This hypothesis, even though derived from a fairly coarse-grained model, is nevertheless plausible, because splitting the cylindrical micelle somewhere along its length would further raise the free energy by creating two spherical caps of even more unfavorable packing geometry (Zhang and Müller, 2017), while the contact between the daughter membranes annihilates the two already existing point defects at the micellar ends.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: When incubating ~60 nm diameter POPC and DOPC vesicles at 18 mM PC, only 2% had completed fusion after 30 min.
source: On the other hand, even when incubating such vesicles at the unusually high concentrations of 18 mM PC, only 2% had completed fusion after 30 min, which does not support the notion of spontaneous fusion—as these authors indeed conclude.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from François-Martin et al. (2017).

claim: The poppase model faces not only kinetic but also equilibrium obstacles.
source: Taken together, our studies support a number of conclusions. To begin with, the poppase model (Stowell et al., 1999) faces not only kinetic but also equilibrium obstacles: extension of the helical scaffold disfavors fission, because a widening groove offsets constriction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: Extension of the helical scaffold disfavors fission because a widening groove offsets constriction.
source: Taken together, our studies support a number of conclusions. To begin with, the poppase model (Stowell et al., 1999) faces not only kinetic but also equilibrium obstacles: extension of the helical scaffold disfavors fission, because a widening groove offsets constriction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: Hemifission is promoted by tilting one of the two symmetry subsets of PH domains.
source: In contrast, hemifission is promoted by tilting one of the two symmetry subsets of PH domains (Mehrotra et al., 2014; Sundborger et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2018), which effectively rotates the filament's adhesive strip away from normal contact.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results, supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Tilting one of the two symmetry subsets of PH domains effectively rotates the filament's adhesive strip away from normal contact.
source: In contrast, hemifission is promoted by tilting one of the two symmetry subsets of PH domains (Mehrotra et al., 2014; Sundborger et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2018), which effectively rotates the filament's adhesive strip away from normal contact.
evidence: This is an inference about how PH domain tilting is represented in the model.

claim: The difference between helical and counter-rotating ring geometries appears not to be central for the role of Darboux torque in fission.
source: The effect is particularly intuitive under mirror symmetry, a geometry at odds with the actual helical one. Surprisingly, this difference appears not to be central.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: Disassembly is essential to complete fission, as argued in the two-stage model.
source: We show that pre-hemifission scaffold breakage aborts fission by allowing the enclosed membrane tube to re-expand. But disassembly is still essential to complete fission, as argued in the two-stage model, because even if the severed bilayer is energetically preferable to the hemifission state (Kozlovsky and Kozlov, 2002), a substantial energy barrier is required to explicitly break the hemifission micelle (Mattila et al., 2015; Zhang and Müller, 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results, supported by citations.

claim: Even if the severed bilayer is energetically preferable to the hemifission state, a substantial energy barrier is required to explicitly break the hemifission micelle.
source: We show that pre-hemifission scaffold breakage aborts fission by allowing the enclosed membrane tube to re-expand. But disassembly is still essential to complete fission, as argued in the two-stage model, because even if the severed bilayer is energetically preferable to the hemifission state (Kozlovsky and Kozlov, 2002), a substantial energy barrier is required to explicitly break the hemifission micelle (Mattila et al., 2015; Zhang and Müller, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanism of completing fission by merging and annihilating the micelle's two endpoint defects is not scaffold specific and may apply to any other fission machinery that leads to a hemifission state involving a small stretch of a cylindrical micelle.
source: Notice that this mechanism is not scaffold specific and may hence apply to any other fission machinery that leads to a hemifission state involving a small stretch of a cylindrical micelle.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generality of the mechanism.

claim: Constriction alone, down to the smallest experimentally observed luminal radii, does not suffice to induce hemifission.
source: How hemifission is induced is experimentally less clear (Antonny et al., 2016). In our studies constriction alone, down to the smallest experimentally observed luminal radii, does not suffice.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: The finding that constriction alone does not suffice to induce hemifission is independent of whether the constricted state is reached passively (two-stage model) or actively (constrictase model).
source: We believe this to be independent of whether the constricted state is reached passively (two-stage model) or actively (constrictase model), since our dynamic protocol could simply be viewed as a means to adiabatically prepare a highly constricted state.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: PH domain tilting emerges as a way to catalyze hemifission.
source: PH domain tilting thus emerges as a way to catalyze hemifission, and since applying a Darboux torque costs energy, we posit that the energy of GTP hydrolysis is at least in part used to drive this conformational change.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: Since applying a Darboux torque costs energy, the energy of GTP hydrolysis is at least in part used to drive the conformational change of PH domain tilting.
source: PH domain tilting thus emerges as a way to catalyze hemifission, and since applying a Darboux torque costs energy, we posit that the energy of GTP hydrolysis is at least in part used to drive this conformational change.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the role of GTP hydrolysis.

claim: The hypothesis that GTP hydrolysis drives PH domain tilting is in accord with experimental findings by Dar and Pucadyil (2017) that replacing the PH domain by a simple binding motif strongly slows down the fission rate.
source: This is in accord with experimental findings by Dar and Pucadyil (2017) that replacing the PH domain by a simple binding motif strongly slows down the fission rate.
evidence: This is a comparison of the hypothesis with experimental evidence, supported by a citation.

claim: The hypothesis that GTP hydrolysis drives PH domain tilting is supported by the Cryo-EM reconstruction by Kong et al. (2018), who suggest that forces generated from the GTPase dimer interaction are transferred across the stalk to the PH domain and from there onto the membrane.
source: It is also supported by the recent Cryo-EM reconstruction by Kong et al. (2018), who suggest that forces generated from the GTPase dimer interaction are transferred across the stalk to the PH domain and from there onto the membrane.
evidence: This is a comparison of the hypothesis with structural evidence, supported by a citation.

claim: In the Cryo-EM reconstruction by Kong et al. (2018), Dyn1 was bound to the nonhydrolyzable guanosine triphosphate analogue GMPPCP, so the question whether GTP hydrolysis would create additional forces or torques remained open.
source: It is worth noting that in their reconstruction Dyn1 was bound to the nonhydrolyzable guanosine triphosphate analogue GMPPCP, and so the question whether GTP hydrolysis would create additional forces or torques that then could be transduced to the membrane remained open.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the structural study, supported by a citation.

claim: To better understand the mechanical basis and viability of force transmission from the GTPase domain to the membrane, it will be essential to structurally resolve the connection between the PH domain to the stalk domain.
source: To better understand the mechanical basis and viability of such a force transmission, it will be essential to structurally resolve the connection between the PH domain to the stalk domain.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Hemifission is consistently initiated by a transient pore puncturing the constricted neck.
source: Finally, we consistently observe that hemifission is initiated by a transient pore puncturing the constricted neck (see arrows in Figure 2h, the time sequence in Figure 4, and Video 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, supported by Figure 2h, Figure 4, and Video 2.

claim: The non-axisymmetric pathway to hemifission via pores is reminiscent of likewise non-axisymmetric pathways seen in fusion simulations.
source: This is reminiscent of likewise non-axisymmetric pathways seen in fusion simulations (Noguchi and Takasu, 2001; Noguchi and Takasu, 2002; Müller et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2003), whose implied transient leakage currents were soon after confirmed to be common in electrophysiological measurements on hemagglutinin-mediated fusion (Frolov et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior simulation and experimental work, supported by citations.

claim: Transient leakage currents implied by non-axisymmetric pathways in fusion simulations were confirmed to be common in electrophysiological measurements on hemagglutinin-mediated fusion.
source: This is reminiscent of likewise non-axisymmetric pathways seen in fusion simulations (Noguchi and Takasu, 2001; Noguchi and Takasu, 2002; Müller et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2003), whose implied transient leakage currents were soon after confirmed to be common in electrophysiological measurements on hemagglutinin-mediated fusion (Frolov et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by a citation.

claim: The pores open to a diameter of no more than 2 nm.
source: We estimate that our pores open to a diameter of no more than 2 nm, which under physiological ionic strength equips them with a conductivity on the order of 1 nS, while their lifetime is a few microseconds (mapped very roughly from our coarse-grained model via lipid self-diffusion).
evidence: This is an estimate from the simulations.

claim: Under physiological ionic strength, the pores have a conductivity on the order of 1 nS.
source: We estimate that our pores open to a diameter of no more than 2 nm, which under physiological ionic strength equips them with a conductivity on the order of 1 nS, while their lifetime is a few microseconds (mapped very roughly from our coarse-grained model via lipid self-diffusion).
evidence: This is an estimate based on the pore size.

claim: The lifetime of the pores is a few microseconds.
source: We estimate that our pores open to a diameter of no more than 2 nm, which under physiological ionic strength equips them with a conductivity on the order of 1 nS, while their lifetime is a few microseconds (mapped very roughly from our coarse-grained model via lipid self-diffusion).
evidence: This is an estimate from the simulations.

claim: Fast transients (few microseconds) have been observed in the gating currents of Shaker potassium channels embedded in Xenopus oocytes, using an eight-pole Bessel filter and achieving a bandwidth of about 200 kHz.
source: This would not be trivial to detect experimentally, but similarly fast transients (few microseconds) have been observed in the gating currents of Shaker potassium channels embedded in Xenopus oocytes, using an eight-pole Bessel filter and achieving a bandwidth of about 200 kHz (Bezanilla, 2018; Sigg and Bezanilla, 2003).
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by citations.

claim: Increasing the ionic strength in reconstituted systems to 1 M could provide a further gain in sensitivity by up to an order of magnitude, provided this does not interfere with dynamin's operation.
source: Increasing the ionic strength in reconstituted systems to 1 M, a further gain in sensitivity by up to an order of magnitude could be obtained, provided this does not interfere with dynamin's operation.
evidence: This is a suggestion for experimental detection.

claim: The leakage pores are partially covered by the dynamin scaffold and, under physiological conditions, possibly by additional proteins proposed to assist in dynamin-driven fission.
source: But notice also that our leakage pores are partially covered by the dynamin scaffold (see again Figure 2h) and, under physiological conditions, possibly by additional proteins proposed to assist in dynamin-driven fission, such as BAR domains (Takei et al., 1999; Farsad et al., 2001; Itoh et al., 2005; Mim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the simulations and knowledge of accessory proteins, supported by Figure 2h and citations.

claim: A pore's effective conductance might be significantly lower than that of a freely accessible membrane pore or channel due to partial coverage by the dynamin scaffold and possibly additional proteins.
source: Hence, a pore's effective conductance might be significantly lower than that of a freely accessible membrane pore or channel.
evidence: This is an inference about the effective conductance.

claim: Pores are larger if hemifission is triggered at larger radii, or if the filament is longer, suggesting that a close coordination of constriction, rotation, and possibly concomitant disassembly renders fission not only more efficient but also more tight.
source: Our simulations show that pores are larger—and hence potential leakage more severe—if hemifission is triggered at larger radii, or if the filament is longer, suggesting that a close coordination of constriction, rotation, and possibly concomitant disassembly renders fission not only more efficient but also more tight.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: Larger pores in mutants disrupting coordination would exacerbate leakage problems and could be experimentally observed.
source: This would exacerbate leakage problems and could be experimentally observed.
evidence: This is a prediction for experimental testing.

claim: All members of the dynamin superfamily are believed to oligomerize, likely into helices.
source: While we have explicitly focused on the case of classical dynamin, several of our findings have implications beyond this particular protein and offer lessons for membrane topology remodeling that go beyond Dyn1. For instance, all members of the dynamin superfamily are believed to oligomerize (Praefcke and McMahon, 2004), likely into helices, for which our generic basic model holds.
evidence: This is a statement about the dynamin superfamily, supported by a citation.

claim: The mismatch between the normal curvature direction of a helical filament and the direction of its adhesive domain will give rise to Darboux torques on the membrane.
source: Whether directly present during assembly or only later triggered by a (possibly GTP-dependent) conformational change, it will give rise to Darboux torques on the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference about the generality of the mechanism.

claim: Darboux torques support the transition into the hemifission state and provide a means to trigger a topological transition that is different from the notions of constriction or elongation.
source: We have explicitly shown that these support the transition into the hemifission state, and hence they provide a means to trigger a topological transition that is different from the notions of constriction or elongation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: Other topology remodeling proteins exist that are unlikely to work by constriction or elongation.
source: This matters because other topology remodeling proteins exist that are unlikely to work by either.
evidence: This is a statement about other proteins, representing general knowledge.

claim: The ESCRT-III complex drives reverse-geometry scission involving the adsorption and polymerization of a helical filament on the inside of the neck to be cut.
source: Consider in particular the reverse-geometry scission driven by the ESCRT-III complex (Wollert et al., 2009), which involves the adsorption and polymerization of a helical filament on the inside of the neck to be cut.
evidence: This is a description of the ESCRT-III complex, supported by a citation.

claim: Present models for ESCRT-III rely on adhesion and/or geometric changes of the spiraling filaments, which result in either direct forces or boundary-induced stresses at the contact site.
source: Present models (for a recent review, see Schöneberg et al. (2017)) rely on adhesion and/or geometric changes of the spiraling filaments, which result in either direct forces or boundary-induced stresses at the contact site (arising from, for instance, a contact curvature condition (Deserno et al., 2007)).
evidence: This is a description of present models, supported by citations.

claim: Geometric rearrangements of a curved elastic filament with a finite twist rigidity, whose material frame is pinned to the membrane, almost invariably result in additional Darboux torques, as well as twist-induced analogs.
source: But geometric rearrangements of a curved elastic filament with a finite twist rigidity, whose material frame is pinned to the membrane (Guven et al., 2014), almost invariably result in additional Darboux torques, as well as twist-induced analogs (Fierling et al., 2016), the relevance of which is only beginning to emerge (Quint et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on theoretical work, supported by citations.

claim: The Darboux torque mechanism is remarkably effective for Dyn1, which suggests that it might be more common than so far realized.
source: In this work we have explicitly demonstrated, for the particular example of Dyn1, that this geometrically elementary mechanism is remarkably effective, which suggest that it might be more common than so far realized: traces of the essential action could date back to the earliest bacterial FtsZ ancestor, which shares many of the key geometric (Erickson, 2000) and biochemical (Lu et al., 2000) features.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generality of the mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: Traces of the Darboux torque mechanism could date back to the earliest bacterial FtsZ ancestor, which shares many of the key geometric and biochemical features with dynamin.
source: In this work we have explicitly demonstrated, for the particular example of Dyn1, that this geometrically elementary mechanism is remarkably effective, which suggest that it might be more common than so far realized: traces of the essential action could date back to the earliest bacterial FtsZ ancestor, which shares many of the key geometric (Erickson, 2000) and biochemical (Lu et al., 2000) features.
evidence: This is a speculation about evolutionary origins, supported by citations.

claim: The Darboux torque mechanism might suggest novel functional models for other membrane remodelers (such as ESCRT-III), for which the mode of operation is much less well understood than for classical dynamin.
source: This might hence suggest novel functional models also for other membrane remodelers (such as ESCRT-III), for which the mode of operation is much less well understood than for classical dynamin.
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability of the mechanism to other proteins.
